chef_bio.background: Founded in Showa 6 (1931) by Aoki Torakichi, who had trained at the kappo restaurant "Uoyasu" in Kanda. When Uoyasu closed following the Great Kanto Earthquake, Aoki went independent and opened his own tempura shop near Kanda Station. That original shop burned down in the Tokyo air raids of WWII, and from 1945 the restaurant has operated continuously at its present site on Suzuran-dori in Jimbocho.
chef_bio.philosophy: The shop's name, "Hachimaki" (headband), comes from words the founder's mentor at Uoyasu gave him when he went independent: that he must work his whole life with a hachimaki tied on, forever training and studying his craft - a philosophy of lifelong dedication that the restaurant has kept as its guiding ethos for over 90 years.
chef_bio.specialty: 穴子海老天丼 (Anago-Ebi Tendon) - a rice bowl topped with two pieces of shrimp tempura, one whole conger eel (anago) tempura, and two pieces of seasonal vegetable tempura, served with miso soup and dressed in a long-simmered tare sauce built on bonito and kelp dashi.

anecdotes.text: The restaurant was a favorite haunt of Showa-era literary and stage giants, including mystery writer Edogawa Ranpo, novelist Ibuse Masuji, playwright Hojo Hideji, and actor Sano Shuji, who all frequented the shop.
Edogawa Ranpo was especially fond of the anago-ebi tendon, the dish credited with hooking generations of regulars and still the restaurant's signature order today.

tokyo3_osteria_lauro.gf_detail: Genuine, real GF item: a weekly-rotating gluten-free FRESH pasta that can be substituted for any pasta dish at dinner for +150 yen (税込). The GF pasta swap addresses the noodle only — sauces, breaded/fried items, the complimentary bread on lunch sets, and flour-dusted prep are all cross-contamination vectors that were NOT confirmed as controlled. There is no published allergen chart and no stated dedicated pot/fryer. Treat as "GF pasta available" not "safe for a sensitive celiac"; a strict celiac should ask (ideally in Japanese) whether the GF pasta is boiled in separate water and whether the chosen sauce is wheat-free.

tokyo3_t_s_kitchen.gf_detail: This is one of the safest GF options in Tokyo for a celiac. It is a fully gluten-free establishment — Asia's first restaurant certified by The Gluten Intolerance Group (GIG) — using NO wheat, barley, or rye anywhere on the premises, plus no chemical seasonings. Because the whole kitchen is wheat-free, the structural wheat traps a celiac normally worries about are removed: soy sauce is gluten-free tamari, ramen uses rice-flour noodles (not wheat), and fried items (karaage, tempura, gyoza) are battered/wrapped in rice flour rather than wheat, so the fryer is not shared with wheat batter. Important caveat the restaurant states itself: some ingredients are sourced from facilities that also process wheat, and they warn that "allergies cannot be guaranteed for all meals due to limited cooking space." So while gluten is structurally excluded, a highly sensitive celiac should still flag their sensitivity when ordering. Note this is NOT a soba shop — the juwari-soba wheat-tsuyu concern does not apply here.
tokyo3_t_s_kitchen.vegan_detail: Vegan is accommodated but this is not a vegan restaurant — the core menu is meat-forward (orange chicken, tonkotsu/pork ramen, chicken ramen, karaage). Dedicated vegan items exist (vegan miso ramen is the flagship vegan dish; vegetarian and pescatarian options are also offered), and staff will accommodate vegan and egg/dairy/nut/soy allergies "to the greatest extent possible." Because many dishes are chicken/pork based and use shared prep space, a vegan should confirm each dish individually. Ask specifically whether the vegan ramen broth is fully plant-based (the restaurant markets no chemical seasonings, but confirm no bonito/katsuo dashi or chicken stock in non-vegan broths bleeding over). Best to state "vegan / bīgan, no meat, no fish, no dashi" when ordering.

chef_bio.background: Founder-owner and chef. Grew up in a food-loving household with a skilled home-cook mother, and learned early that 'people naturally smile when they eat something delicious.' Her focus on gluten-free began during time spent in the United States, where she saw abundant, genuinely good gluten-free restaurants — a stark contrast to Japan, where at the time people with gluten intolerance had largely resigned themselves to giving up delicious food. She has researched gluten-free cooking for over 10 years (sparked by a friend's illness) and has done recipe development and consulting on food diversity and allergy accommodation for major companies before opening her own restaurant.
chef_bio.philosophy: To turn dietary restriction into possibility — 食の制限から、可能性を味わうレストラン ('from restriction to tasting possibility'). She wants the restaurant to be 'a catalyst for smiles' for people who need gluten-free diets, proving GF food can be both safe and delicious through continuous recipe and product development.
chef_bio.specialty: Certified fully gluten-free Japanese/Asian comfort food: rice-flour ramen (incl. a vegan miso ramen), orange chicken, rice-flour chicken gyoza, karaage and tempura battered in rice flour, plus a morning menu — all wheat/barley/rye-free.

anecdotes.text: Her restaurant is the first in Asia to earn gluten-free certification from The Gluten Intolerance Group (GIG), the US-based certifier — the credential she pursued specifically so that celiac diners could trust the kitchen rather than take a menu's word for it.
She cites that the Kanto region alone has over 210,000 people with gluten intolerance, many of whom had given up on eating out — the gap she opened the restaurant to close.

The concept grew into a small group: the Ueno-Hirokoji branch (opened March 2024, inside APA Hotel Ueno Hirokoji), the original Roppongi restaurant, and a gluten-free izakaya in Harajuku opening April 2026.

chef_bio.background: A Tokyo homemaker who by her own account loved marbled toro, sirloin steak and other rich meat and dairy before founding the company. chef_bio.philosophy: 'Smile-veg' (スマイルベジ) — food should let everyone, whatever their diet, sit at the same table and say 'this is delicious' together. She frames health-through-food as prevention in daily eating rather than something you turn to only after falling ill, and wanted a welcoming shared space rather than merely a cookbook.

Within five days in late May 2009 chance meetings with a photographer and a designer led her to the Jiyugaoka location and a team; strikingly, the logo approval (25 Jun), handover (25 Aug) and opening (25 Sep 2009) all landed on the 25th.

chef_bio.chef_name: Rajendra Jain (ラジェンドラ・ジェイン)

tokyo3__225.gf_detail: Explicitly markets a "ヴィーガン&グルテンフリーの本格和食コース." Owner-chef Kawahara spent ~a year rebuilding the kitchen's foundation for plant-based cooking and states he "systematically reviewed all seasonings and ingredients," and the vegetable course "がグルテンフリーにも対応できるようになりました" (can now be made gluten-free). Strong points for a celiac: it is a reservation-only, made-to-order 9-seat counter with no same-day service (nothing pre-batched), and GF is arranged as a deliberate advance accommodation rather than a substitution on the fly — so the kitchen knows in advance. IMPORTANT to confirm at booking: the site does NOT explicitly state that a wheat-free (tamari) soy sauce is used, and standard Japanese shoyu/mirin/miso and any wheat-containing seasoning is the main gluten risk in a course like this. When you reserve, state coeliac/セリアック and ask them to confirm wheat-free soy sauce (小麦不使用の醤油/たまり) and no wheat in any seasoning. No juwari-soba issue here — this is a vegetable kaiseki, not a soba shop. GF is request-based, so treat it as a confirmed accommodation you must arrange in advance, not a walk-in guarantee.
tokyo3__225.vegan_detail: A complete multi-course vegan kaiseki is offered (Vegetable Full Course ~12 items ¥9,500; Short Course ~8 items ¥5,500). Dashi is the key win: the site states "出汁は昆布と野菜のみで丁寧に取り、動物性のものは使用しておりません" (broth made only from kombu and vegetables; no animal products) — so no hidden bonito/katsuo dashi, which is the usual trap in Japanese vegetable cooking. No meat, fish, or eggs in the vegan course; monthly rotating seasonal-vegetable menu. Note: the restaurant ALSO runs a separate standard (non-vegan) 味農家 course that includes animal products, so it is not an all-vegan house — the vegan course is a distinct, fully plant-based menu you must order/reserve. Allium-free (五葷抜き) can be accommodated with advance notice.

chef_bio.background: Unusual second-career chef. Studied industrial/applied chemistry at university and worked in the semiconductor industry before changing course at age 30. He then enrolled at Hattori Nutrition College (服部栄養専門学校) and trained for about six years at a kaiseki restaurant in Yanaka before opening Minoya in June 2008. For roughly six years he also ran his own vegetable farm in Koshigaya, Saitama, to deepen his understanding of produce.
chef_bio.philosophy: Cook to 'draw out' (引き出す) each vegetable's own aroma, texture and umami through classical Japanese technique rather than mask it. He deliberately never repeats a course — the menu rotates monthly with the seasons so returning guests always get something new.
chef_bio.specialty: Vegan and gluten-free Japanese kaiseki built entirely from seasonal vegetables, anchored by a house dashi he developed over about a year from kombu and vegetable trimmings to replace fish-based stock. Roughly 30 vegetable ingredients per course, ~600 kcal total.

anecdotes.text: Kawahara started from a chemistry and semiconductor career, then pivoted at 30 to train at Hattori Nutrition College and a Yanaka kaiseki house before opening Minoya in 2008.

When he began building vegetarian menus around 2014 he found dashi the biggest obstacle — '和食の場合、一番のネックが出汁になります' — and spent about a year developing a custom kombu-and-vegetable-scrap dashi, then reviewed every seasoning, offering fully vegan-compatible kaiseki from 2017.
He kept his own vegetable farm in Koshigaya, Saitama for about six years and refuses to serve the same course twice, changing the menu monthly to keep regulars engaged.

tokyo3__236.gf_detail: Not a GF-focused or dedicated GF kitchen — treat as "some naturally GF items, ask carefully." Naturally gluten-free choices exist because much South Indian food here is rice/lentil based: dosa and idli are made from fermented rice + urad (black gram) batter, and plain rice, sambar, rassam, dal and most curries are wheat-free by tradition. REAL WHEAT RISKS to raise with staff: (1) naan, chapati/roti, paratha and puri are wheat — the kitchen dusts and rolls wheat flour in the same small space, so flour-dust cross-contact on other plates is plausible; (2) the Indo-Chinese section (chow mein / "chowmein", Manchurian, Hakka noodles) uses wheat noodles and wheat-based soy sauce; (3) samosa pastry is wheat and if it shares the fryer oil with pakora/bonda/vada, that oil is cross-contaminated — confirm whether the fryer is shared (unknown, see safety); (4) asafoetida (hing), a near-ubiquitous South Indian spice, is very commonly cut with wheat flour — a hidden gluten source in dal/sambar/chutneys that most staff won't flag unless asked directly. No juwari-soba issue here (not a soba shop). A celiac can likely eat well (rice + dal + plain dosa) but MUST ask about hing and the fryer; there is no allergen sheet evidence found.
tokyo3__236.vegan_detail: Establishment is 100% vegetarian (no meat, no fish, no egg) — so no hidden bonito/katsuo dashi or fish-sauce trap that plagues Japanese kitchens; this is Indian cooking. However it is LACTO-vegetarian, not vegan by default: paneer, ghee (clarified butter), butter, cream and yogurt/curd (and lassi) appear widely, and plain naan is typically brushed with butter/ghee. Vegan-safe items are marked with a green dot on the menu and staff will identify them, but you must ask. Reliable vegan picks reported: dosa and other rice/lentil dishes, dal, chana/aloo chana chaat, pani puri, baingan bharta, sambar/rassam, and "keema" made from soy mince / soy meatballs (大豆ミート). Confirm no ghee/cream/yogurt on the specific dish and ask for oil instead of ghee.

chef_bio.background: Family-run Indian vegetarian specialty restaurant that opened in 2014 in Taito-ku (east side of Okachimachi/Ueno). Indian-owned and operated, with Hindi spoken in-house and a following among the local Indian community. It has been selected multiple times (reported as six times) as a Tabelog Hyakumeiten (Top-100 curry) restaurant.
chef_bio.philosophy: '菜食中心' — vegetarian-centred Indian cooking that aims to satisfy as full Indian cuisine rather than as compromise 'veggie food'; no meat or fish used at all, with plant-based (vegan) options flagged on the menu.
chef_bio.specialty: South Indian dosa (notably an all-the-way crispy, パリパリ style, ~45cm) and thali/meals, alongside North Indian naan-and-curry and Indo-Chinese dishes; soy-'meat' keema.

anecdotes.text: A Tabelog Hyakumeiten (Top-100) regular, reported as selected six times since opening in 2014; its dosa is distinctive for a deliberately crunchy, entirely-crispy texture rather than the usual soft-and-crisp.

tokyo3__280.gf_detail: No dedicated gluten-free kitchen, no GF claim on the shop's own website or in its interviews — the "グルテンフリー対応" tag comes only from aggregators, not the restaurant. Treat as ASK/celiac-caution. Concrete wheat/barley risks found in the actual menu: several deli items are soy-sauce-based (e.g. the bulgogi and various marinades), and standard Japanese soy sauce contains wheat; the signature side is 国産雑穀米 (domestic multigrain rice), which commonly includes 押し麦/barley — a gluten grain — so the base rice itself is a likely risk and must be checked. Food is deli-style (roasted, marinated, salads) rather than deep-fried, so batter/shared-fryer risk is low, but prep surfaces and serving are shared across all items in the deli case. A celiac should point to specific items and confirm each one with staff (who do know their ingredients, since everything is handmade in-house); do not assume any plate is safe by default. Naturally lower-risk candidates to ask about: the green salad with a non-soy house dressing, the radicchio-and-mushroom quinoa salad, and the root-vegetable & chickpea spice roast — but verify the seasoning on each.
tokyo3__280.vegan_detail: Genuine vegan and vegetarian deli items are available and rotate daily; per the official Chiyoda city tourism listing, staff can tell you which of the 10+ daily deli items are vegan (no animal-derived ingredients) and which are vegetarian. However this is NOT a vegan restaurant — the deli case is mostly omnivore (bulgogi, low-temp pork roast, mackerel herb marinade, chicken thigh, Spanish omelet, scallop and octopus marinades) and two of the four salad dressings contain dairy (balsamic-cheese, yogurt). Choose the plainly plant-based sides (e.g. root-vegetable & chickpea spice roast, radicchio-mushroom quinoa salad, avocado salsa) plus the green salad with an apple or carrot (non-dairy) dressing. Watch for hidden animal stock/fish in marinades and dashi in the seasoning — ask per item. A vegan can eat well here by picking the right sides, but must confirm choices with staff each visit.

Ingredients are organic/low-pesticide vegetables, mechanically pressed rapeseed and extra-virgin olive oil only, Italian sea salt and cane sugar, domestic multigrain rice, everything handmade with no preservatives or chemical seasonings.

chef_bio.background: The shop's predecessor, 中国料理中本, opened in September 1968 near Kami-Itabashi Station, founded by 中本正 (originally as a borscht-serving eatery, ボルシチの店 中本). Nakamoto pursued intensely spicy dishes rarely seen in other restaurants at the time. The shop closed in December 1998 for the founder's health. A devoted customer of ~20 years, 白根誠, repeatedly asked to inherit the shop, was refused, then trained under Nakamoto and reopened it as 蒙古タンメン中本 in 2000. It is now operated by Shirane's company, 株式会社誠フードサービス, across multiple Tokyo/Kanto branches.

Today the branches are run by Shirane's 株式会社誠フードサービス, which grew the once-single shop into one of Tokyo's best-known spicy-ramen chains.
